item.title: The Bytes Moved, the Compute Didn't: Ten Years of Path Dependence in Decentralized Databases
item.description: 中文版是这篇文章的默认版本。 阅读中文版 → This English page stays available at this URL; the Chinese version is the one we maintain first. In one line: the field’s unsolved problem is not that consensus is too weak, it is that compute never followed the bytes. A database is not one thing — it is four: write order, byte location, execution location, read permission. Six routes, and each one bought exactly one of them.

item.title: The Database Got a New User: Record Stores and Context Layers for Agents
item.description: 中文版是这篇文章的默认版本。 阅读中文版 → This English page stays available at this URL; the Chinese version is the one we maintain first. In one line: the database’s main user stopped being a person, so it grew a second leg — one that holds state and provisions on demand, one that supplies context and compiles it ahead of the query. What really changed is the definition of retrieval: from a recall algorithm to an orchestration frame plus a compiled supply.

item.title: The Architecture of Trust: A Research Report on Web3.0 Database and Storage Systems
item.description: tap to enlarge Section 1: Introduction - The Paradigm Shift from Centralized to Decentralized Data# The evolution of the internet can be demarcated into distinct architectural and philosophical eras. The current dominant paradigm, Web 2.0, is defined by interactive, user-driven platforms that have connected the globe. However, this model is predicated on a fundamental asymmetry: while users create the content and data, centralized corporations own the platforms, control the data, and capture the vast majority of the economic value.
